title: Evidence-Tiering of Culturally Sensitive Vaccine Confidence Interventions in Nigeria
content: Vaccine hesitancy remains a substantial barrier to immunisation coverage in Nigeria, with a documented historical dimension rooted in the 1996 Trovan trial and its continuing influence on subsequent vaccine campaigns. Programme designers have increasingly turned to culturally embedded intervention models combining trusted local messengers, digital outreach, and narrative-based messaging, but these mechanisms are not equally supported by outcome evidence. This article reviews Nigeria-specific evidence for five recurrent mechanisms identified in programme proposals and grey literature. Two, trusted-messenger engagement and structured digital campaigns, have trial-level support, including a cluster-randomised controlled trial showing substantially higher vaccination odds and a nationally randomised social media evaluation showing measurable reductions in hesitancy. Two others, AI-driven sentiment monitoring and folklore-embedded messaging, remain commonly proposed but empirically untested. We argue that proposal review processes should explicitly grade mechanisms by evidentiary strength, anchoring core design in trial-supported approaches while treating less-evidenced components as piloted, measured additions.
